questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I was attracted to the multicultural aspect of Hong Kong, and I wanted to explore that. I had already known that I wanted to go there back when I was in high school, so it was merely about finding the right time to do so.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: HKU is quite helpful, although it is very easy to become overwhelmed with the constant updates about everything and the events. You need to have a good head on your shoulders to organize all of the information yourself too.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: HKU provided us with some information for finding our way to the dorms, in the form of instructions on how to get a cab from the airport. They sent out a bunch of information about how our dorm rooms work, and step by step on formal procedures before settling in, plus rules.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: There were some events in the beginning for exchange students, but gradually, it sort of weaned and you had to quickly figure out what was tailored to locals and what was tailored to exchange students. I know some of my friends joined clubs they thought would be international since HKU is an English school, but the club activities were conducted in Cantonese. That was a bit of a wake-up call.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: My dorms weren't exactly on campus; we still had a good 30-40 minutes away by bus/train, but it was the only dorm to offer individual rooms, so no roommates. Many of us exchange students weren't used to sharing a bedroom, so we sort of unknowingly all flocked to the same dorm. If you're willing to sleep in the same room with another student, you'll have tons of options.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: There was a kitchen on each floor, which we would share. About 20 people were sharing the kitchen, but we didn't have much of a problem besides an infestation of weevils, so everyone had to throw out their bread, rice, and pasta. After that, we started to keep the food in our rooms and didn't have a problem. I was very lucky; my floor didn't have a problem with thieves, but I know from my friends that they had massive issues with food theft, so beware.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Unless you live in Jockey 4 (my dorms and the newest built ones), prepare to live with mold. Some of the dorms have problems with hazing activities as well. especially those more geared towards the locals. My advice would be to pick Jockey 4. Most exchange students live there, but there are also locals, which is super nice, so you're not in a constant foreigner bubble. It also depends on your floor, really; I know some floors, such as mine, had a way better social life than others. Some people choose to sit inside their rooms because it is not a requirement to socialize at Jockey 4, but if you wish to meet new people, the best way is to arrive, sit out in the kitchen, simply greet people as they and chat with others, it helps a lot. With Jockey 4, you get the newly built amenities. Most likely, your exchange friends will live there as well, making it easier, but of course, you must accept the travel time to get to campus.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Relatively easy, the website is sort of outdated but it didn't really matter. We had a add-on drop-off period which i used to drop some courses i found out weren't really for me anyway. Everything works pretty efficiently.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: During the orientation week, we were supplied with various emails we could get in contact with for help.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got the majority i wished for, although i was denied some which i struggled to understand why because they didn't state a reason.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Make sure to check again and again whether a course you want is available. I wished to sign up for a criminology course that was full, but when i checked in later it was open again because someone dropped it. So make sure to check a second time.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level was okay, it wasn't particularly harder than KU, nor was it easier. Some courses had very loose expectations. All of the courses I took had mandatory attendance, plus they expected us to complete all the assignments, presentations, in-class tests, reports, and portfolios. To say that it was overwhelming is an understatement. Even if it was easier, I feel like I did more in a semester at HKU than I've done in my entire time at HKU. I wanted to tell them, "Sheer output is not a good measure of talent. How am I supposed to write anything good if I have 10 other reports to complete at the exact same time?" enough said.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Most of my professors were well-educated and seemed very knowledgeable about their study of the field. I enjoyed the discussions we had, even though, at times, it felt like they delegated their work to their PhD students who weren't quite on their level yet.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: GLAS 3102 The EU as a global actor: Amazing and attentive professor, his classes were a joy to attend. We had great discussions in class, and I truly felt like I learned so much in a short span of time. The class is also smaller, so it's much easier to facilitate debates.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Student activities are not cheap! It costs a ton of money if you wish to attend student parties, go out to dinner with your new friends, or even join a sport. Hong Kong is the most expensive place in Asia to live for a reason.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Public transport is super affordable! The phone bill was quite inexpensive, too. What was more expensive than expected was food. One would think eating out is expensive, but surely making your own food is less. Nope, both are just expensive. Everything is expensive. If you want to go to Hong Kong and eat Western food, buy pasta or bread from the supermarket, think again: unless you're a millionaire or something.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There were a bunch of things. Hiking groups and sports to join, such as archery and tennis. There were also art clubs and language clubs. Of course, most of it is suited for locals since the vast majority is conducted in Cantonese. I wanted to sign up for archery but had no way to do so because they requested payment via an app that requires a Hong Kong credit card, which I couldn't get because I was only there for one semester.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Go to the parties, even if they lowkey suck most of the time, you'll still get to hang out with your friends and also meet a bunch of other people along the way.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go and visit the smaller islands of Hong Kong, there are so many! and they differ a lot from the main island, so go and explore to your heart's content.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was quite easy for me since i had already been on exchange to a different asian country, so i sort of knew what to expect.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Don't start out the conversation by discussing politics; it's a super sensitive topic. Just be open and follow their lead. Most locals are afraid of messing up in English when speaking with us exchange students, so just be nice and patient.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The public spitting, the constant crowding of people wherever you go. I swear, here back home, we have rush hour, right? Hong Kong rush hour is 24/7; don't panic when in tight crowds. Just move along with the wave of people, and please don't fall. Also, people will stare, they have no shame about it, especially older men, just stare back. Also, accept the fact that awareness of your surroundings is overrated; people will stop in the middle of the road to look at their phones, and they will also stand right behind you when you're getting money from an ATM.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Hong Kong people are open to sharing their culture with others, which is great. Everyone speaks English, too, to varying degrees, but it's still understandable and helpful. People are generally kind, and because Hong Kong has so many foreigners, you typically won't feel out of place. I felt at home.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Save as much money as you can in advance, you will need it. 
2. Choose a dorm, finding an apartment by yourself is nearly impossible and just not worth it (unless you're going on an exchange with your partner)
3. Explore Hong Kong, whether that be by yourself or with other exchange students. There are so many sights to catch.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Nothing i haven't already mentioned yet.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: I genuinely feel as if I have grown and matured as a person. Now, whenever I get anxious about doing something trivial back home, I remind myself, "You've lived in Hong Kong, if you can do that, you can do this." It actually works!

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: People can be complicated. You're gonna meet folks whom you probably don't like very much, but that's just part of life. Someone might hurt your feelings, but it happens, and you have to move past it. I would remind myself that literally everyone is confused about everything and no one knows what they're doing when they're on exchange. It was my first time studying at HKU, and the same goes for all of my friends.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
